causal_claim: Long Short-Term Memory made the Transformer architecture possible by proving long-range sequence dependencies could be learned, defining the long-context problem whose sequential, non-parallel training the Transformer then removed.
definition: A gated recurrent network by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber that preserves error flow over more than 1,000 time steps.
name: Long Short-Term Memory (1997)

causal_claim: Sequence-to-sequence learning made the Transformer architecture possible by supplying the encoder-decoder template the Transformer kept, while its fixed-vector bottleneck and sequential LSTM encoding motivated replacing recurrence with attention.
definition: Sutskever, Vinyals and Le's end-to-end encoder-decoder framework mapping an input sequence to an output sequence with LSTMs.
name: Sequence-to-sequence learning (2014)
source_title: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks

causal_claim: Attention mechanism (Bahdanau) made the Transformer architecture possible by showing a model could dispense with a single fixed-length vector and instead weight all source positions, the operation the Transformer generalized into self-attention as its sole sequence mixer.
definition: Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio's soft alignment that lets a decoder form a fresh weighted sum of encoder states for each output word.
name: Attention mechanism (Bahdanau) (2014)

causal_claim: Gated Recurrent Unit made the Transformer architecture possible by demonstrating in the 2014 encoder-decoder translation systems that gated units captured long dependencies, sharpening the state of the art whose sequential computation the Transformer had to beat in parallel.
definition: Cho et al.'s simplified gated recurrent unit with update and reset gates, comparable to LSTM with fewer parameters.
name: Gated Recurrent Unit (2014)
source_title: Empirical Evaluation of Gated Recurrent Neural Networks on Sequence Modeling

causal_claim: ByteNet made the Transformer architecture possible by proving a non-recurrent, parallelizable convolutional sequence model could beat recurrent translation models, directly attacking the RNN serial bottleneck the Transformer also removed.
definition: Kalchbrenner et al.'s dilated convolutional encoder-decoder for translation that runs in linear time and preserves temporal resolution.
name: ByteNet (2016)
source_title: Neural Machine Translation in Linear Time

causal_claim: Word2vec embeddings made the Transformer architecture possible by establishing learned dense token embeddings as the standard input representation, which the Transformer adopts as its embedding layer added to positional encodings.
definition: Mikolov et al.'s efficient CBOW and skip-gram methods for learning dense continuous word vectors from billions of words.
name: Word2vec embeddings (2013)
source_title: Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space

causal_claim: Deep Residual Learning (ResNet) made the Transformer architecture possible by supplying the residual shortcut connections wrapped around every Transformer sub-layer, enabling deep stacks to train without degradation.
definition: He et al.'s residual learning framework where layers fit F(x)=H(x)-x and add their input back via identity shortcuts.
name: Deep Residual Learning (ResNet) (2015)
source_title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition

causal_claim: Layer Normalization made the Transformer architecture possible by providing the per-example normalization used in every Transformer block to stabilize hidden dynamics independent of batch size.
definition: Ba, Kiros and Hinton's normalization computing mean and variance over all summed inputs in a layer for a single training case.
name: Layer Normalization (2016)

causal_claim: Dropout made the Transformer architecture possible by providing the regularization applied in its attention, feed-forward and residual paths, allowing a large translation model to generalize from WMT data.
definition: Srivastava et al.'s regularization that randomly drops units during training to prevent co-adaptation and overfitting.
name: Dropout (2014)
source_title: Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting

causal_claim: GloVe made the Transformer architecture possible by reinforcing that token meaning lives in a learned vector space structured by dot products, the same dot-product geometry the Transformer's scaled dot-product attention and embeddings exploit.
definition: Pennington, Socher and Manning's global log-bilinear regression model learning word vectors from global co-occurrence counts.
name: GloVe (2014)
source_title: Glove: Global Vectors for Word Representation

causal_claim: Cross-entropy loss made the Transformer architecture possible by giving its softmax output over the vocabulary a principled training objective, so next-token and translation training is maximum-likelihood estimation.
definition: The expected cost of encoding data from distribution p with a code optimized for model q, equal to negative log-likelihood as a training loss.
name: Cross-entropy loss (1948)
source_title: Cross-Entropy and the Cross-Entropy Loss – AI in Action

causal_claim: Gradient descent made the Transformer architecture possible by supplying the first-order optimization principle, in stochastic and Adam variants, by which all Transformer parameters are trained.
definition: Cauchy's iterative method for minimizing a function by stepping in the direction of the negative gradient.
name: Gradient descent (1847)

causal_claim: Linnainmaa's automatic differentiation made the Transformer architecture possible by providing the reverse-mode gradient computation implemented in modern frameworks that train the Transformer's attention projections.
definition: Linnainmaa's reverse mode of automatic differentiation, computing derivatives of nested differentiable functions by propagating errors backward through a graph.
name: Linnainmaa's automatic differentiation (1970)

causal_claim: Backpropagation made the Transformer architecture possible by making end-to-end training of deep multi-layer networks practical, including jointly training attention alignment with the rest of the model as later Transformer training requires.
definition: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams' procedure for adjusting network weights by back-propagating output errors so hidden units learn representations.
name: Backpropagation (1986)

causal_claim: A Mathematical Theory of Communication made the Transformer architecture possible by founding the probabilistic view of language as a distribution over symbols, from which the Transformer's softmax probabilities, entropy and perplexity evaluation derive.
definition: Shannon's founding information theory introducing entropy as the measure of uncertainty and the limits of lossless encoding.
name: A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948)

causal_claim: CUDA made the Transformer architecture possible by exposing thousands of GPU cores for the dense matrix multiplications of attention, making parallel-over-sequence training computationally feasible.
definition: NVIDIA's parallel computing platform and API, released February 16, 2007, letting GPUs be used for general-purpose computation.
name: CUDA (2007)

causal_claim: TensorFlow made the Transformer architecture possible by providing the dataflow framework with automatic differentiation and GPU distribution in which the original Transformer was implemented and trained.
definition: Google Brain's open-source machine learning system, released November 9, 2015, for expressing and executing dataflow computations on heterogeneous hardware.
name: TensorFlow (2015)
source_title: TensorFlow: Large-Scale Machine Learning on Heterogeneous Distributed Systems

causal_claim: ImageNet made the Transformer architecture possible by proving large labeled benchmarks plus GPU training could drive deep-network breakthroughs, creating the benchmark-and-scale culture and GPU practice later applied to translation.
definition: Deng et al.'s large-scale hierarchical image database of 3.2 million images in 5,247 WordNet synsets presented at CVPR 2009.
name: ImageNet (2009)
source_title: ImageNet: A Large-Scale Hierarchical Image Database

causal_claim: WMT made the Transformer architecture possible by supplying the standardized WMT'14 English-German and English-French benchmarks on which the Transformer was defined and claimed state of the art.
definition: The first WMT workshop and shared translation task, held in 2006, comparing machine translation systems on common Europarl data.
name: WMT Workshop on Statistical Machine Translation (2006)
source_title: Ten Years of WMT Evaluation Campaigns: Lessons Learnt

causal_claim: BLEU score made the Transformer architecture possible by giving translation research a cheap, reproducible yardstick, the exact metric the Transformer paper used to demonstrate superiority over recurrent and convolutional models.
definition: Papineni et al.'s automatic machine translation metric based on clipped n-gram precision against human references with a brevity penalty.
name: BLEU score (2002)

causal_claim: Penn Treebank made the Transformer architecture possible by pioneering large tokenized, annotated text corpora as training and test material for statistical language models, the substrate paradigm sequence models including Transformers depend on.
definition: Marcus, Santorini and Marcinkiewicz's corpus of over 4.5 million words of American English annotated with part-of-speech tags and skeletal syntax.
name: Penn Treebank (1993)
source_title: Building a Large Annotated Corpus of English: The Penn Treebank

causal_claim: Europarl corpus made the Transformer architecture possible by providing the sentence-aligned parallel text that trained and evaluated the WMT translation pipeline from which the Transformer's task, data format and baselines came.
definition: Koehn's parallel corpus of European Parliament proceedings in 11 languages, about 30 million words per language, for statistical machine translation.
name: Europarl corpus (2005)
source_title: Europarl: A Parallel Corpus for Statistical Machine Translation

causal_claim: Common Crawl made the Transformer architecture possible by creating a freely available web-scale text substrate, demonstrating that massive raw corpora could be collected and shared for training data-hungry sequence models.
definition: A nonprofit founded in 2007 by Gil Elbaz that crawls the web and freely provides petabyte-scale archives of web pages to the public.
name: Common Crawl (2007)

causal_claim: One Billion Word Benchmark made the Transformer architecture possible by normalizing billion-word tokenized corpora and perplexity comparison at scale, showing sequence models improved with data volume as Transformer training assumes.
definition: Chelba et al.'s benchmark corpus with almost one billion words of training data for measuring progress in statistical language modeling.
name: One Billion Word Benchmark (2013)
source_title: One Billion Word Benchmark for Measuring Progress in Statistical Language Modeling

causal_claim: BookCorpus made the Transformer architecture possible by providing long, contiguous narrative text suitable for learning sentence and long-context representations, the kind of long-sequence material recurrent models struggled with and Transformers were built to exploit.
definition: Zhu et al.'s dataset of around 11,038 free books containing 984 million words, introduced for aligning books and movies.
name: BookCorpus (2015)

causal_claim: Bayes' theorem made the Transformer architecture possible by supplying the conditional-probability calculus in which next-token prediction, the Transformer's training task, is formulated.
definition: A rule for computing a conditional probability distribution from a prior distribution and the likelihood of observed evidence.
name: Bayes' theorem (1763)

causal_claim: Matrix algebra (Cayley) made the Transformer architecture possible by defining the matrix multiplication from which every query, key, value and feed-forward computation in a Transformer block is built.
definition: Arthur Cayley's 1858 memoir gave the first abstract definition of a matrix and defined matrix addition, multiplication, scalar multiplication and inverses.
name: Matrix algebra (Cayley) (1858)

causal_claim: Gradient descent made the Transformer architecture possible by providing the optimization principle used to fit its millions of weights to a language-modeling loss.
definition: Augustin-Louis Cauchy's 1847 iterative method for minimizing a differentiable function by stepping in the direction of the negative gradient.
name: Gradient descent (1847)

causal_claim: Boltzmann distribution made the Transformer architecture possible by giving the exponential-normalized form that the softmax in its attention weights and output layer directly instantiates, with scores in place of energies.
definition: Ludwig Boltzmann's 1868 probability distribution assigning each state a probability proportional to the exponential of its negative energy divided by temperature.
name: Boltzmann distribution (1868)

causal_claim: Cross-entropy loss made the Transformer architecture possible by serving as the exact objective minimized when a Transformer is trained to predict the next token.
definition: The information-theoretic measure, rooted in Claude Shannon's 1948 theory, of the average negative log-probability a predicted distribution assigns to outcomes drawn from a target distribution.
name: Cross-entropy loss (1948)

causal_claim: GeForce 256 made the Transformer architecture possible by establishing the GPU as a distinct parallel processor class, the hardware lineage whose dense matrix throughput Transformers require because they abandoned sequential recurrence for parallel matrix operations.
definition: NVIDIA's 1999 GeForce 256, marketed as the world's first GPU, a single-chip processor with integrated transform, lighting, triangle setup and rendering engines.
name: GeForce 256 (1999)

causal_claim: arXiv made the Transformer architecture possible by creating the rapid preprint channel through which its predecessor results in attention, sequence-to-sequence learning and optimization circulated and on which 'Attention Is All You Need' itself was first published.
definition: Paul Ginsparg's open-access preprint repository, launched on August 14, 1991 at Los Alamos, for circulating scientific papers before journal publication.
name: arXiv (1991)

causal_claim: Amazon EC2 made the Transformer architecture possible by making large fleets of rented compute, including GPU instances, available on demand, so training a compute-hungry parallel architecture no longer required owning a supercomputer.
definition: Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud, launched in public beta on August 25, 2006, which lets users rent virtual computers by the hour to run their own applications.
name: Amazon EC2 (2006)

causal_claim: CUDA made the Transformer architecture possible by exposing GPU parallelism to general code, and the Transformer's design bet — replacing sequential recurrence with large parallelizable matrix multiplications — only pays off on CUDA-programmable hardware.
definition: NVIDIA's parallel computing platform and API, officially released in February 2007, that lets software use GPUs for general-purpose accelerated processing.
name: CUDA (2007)

causal_claim: TensorFlow made the Transformer architecture possible by providing the automatic-differentiation, GPU and distributed-training framework in which the original Transformer was implemented and trained at Google.
definition: Google Brain's open-source machine learning library, released under the Apache 2.0 license on November 9, 2015, for expressing and executing dataflow computations on heterogeneous hardware.
name: TensorFlow (2015)

causal_claim: Broadbent's filter model of attention made the Transformer architecture possible by originating the psychology concept of attention as selective allocation of limited processing capacity that neural attention mechanisms, and hence the Transformer, borrowed by name and function.
definition: Donald Broadbent's 1958 early-selection theory that a selective filter admits only one channel of sensory information into a limited-capacity processing system.
name: Broadbent's filter model of attention (1958)

causal_claim: Hubel and Wiesel receptive fields made the Transformer architecture possible by establishing the hierarchical feature-detection model of cortex that inspired convolutional and layered neural architectures, the vision tradition from which multi-head attention's multiple parallel feature channels descend.
definition: David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel's 1962 finding that visual cortex neurons respond selectively to oriented edges, with simple cells built from aligned inputs and complex cells pooling simple cells.
name: Hubel and Wiesel receptive fields (1962)
source_title: Neural Mechanisms for the Generation of Visual Complex Cells

causal_claim: IBM Models of statistical machine translation made the Transformer architecture possible by formalizing alignment between source and target words as a probabilistic object, the direct ancestor of the learned soft alignments that became attention in neural translation and then self-attention.
definition: Brown and colleagues' 1993 series of five statistical translation models that define a word-by-word alignment between sentence pairs and assign a probability to each alignment.
name: IBM Models of statistical machine translation (1993)
source_title: The Mathematics of Statistical Machine Translation: Parameter Estimation

causal_claim: Posner cueing paradigm made the Transformer architecture possible by demonstrating experimentally that attention is a movable, measurable allocation that can be directed to a location before a stimulus arrives, the cognitive framing later formalized as query-driven attention weighting in the Transformer.
definition: Michael Posner's 1980 'Orienting of Attention' paradigm measuring, via valid and invalid spatial cues, how covertly shifting attention speeds or slows target detection.
name: Posner cueing paradigm (1980)
source_title: ORIENTING OF ATTENTION: THEN AND NOW

causal_claim: Attention mechanism (Bahdanau) made the Transformer architecture possible by proving that learned soft alignment weights could replace a fixed-length sentence vector; the Transformer generalized that alignment into self-attention and discarded the recurrent encoder-decoder around it.
definition: Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio's 2014 mechanism in which a translation decoder computes, for each output word, a softmax-weighted sum of encoder states via a jointly learned alignment model.
name: Attention mechanism (Bahdanau) (2014)

causal_claim: Linnainmaa's automatic differentiation made the Transformer architecture possible by making it computationally feasible to get exact gradients for every one of a Transformer's weights in a single backward pass through its attention and feed-forward graph.
definition: Seppo Linnainmaa's 1970 reverse mode of automatic differentiation, which computes the derivative of a composite function represented as a graph by recursively applying the chain rule in reverse.
name: Linnainmaa's automatic differentiation (1970)

causal_claim: Backpropagation made the Transformer architecture possible by establishing the routine end-to-end training procedure by which a Transformer's embeddings, attention projections and feed-forward layers all learn their representations jointly from the next-token error signal.
definition: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams' 1986 Nature paper popularizing back-propagation, repeatedly adjusting network weights to minimize output error so hidden units learn internal representations.
name: Backpropagation (Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams) (1986)
source_title: Learning representations by back-propagating errors - ADS

causal_claim: Glorot initialization made the Transformer architecture possible by solving the variance blow-up and vanishing that otherwise prevent training deep stacks, and its variance argument is the same reasoning behind the Transformer's scaling of query-key dot products by the square root of the key dimension.
definition: Glorot and Bengio's 2010 initialization scheme scaling random weights by fan-in and fan-out to keep activation and gradient variances stable across layers of a deep network.
name: Glorot initialization (2010)
source_title: Understanding the difficulty of training deep feedforward neural networks

causal_claim: Dropout made the Transformer architecture possible by providing the regularizer applied inside the original Transformer's attention and feed-forward sublayers, without which its large parameter count overfit the translation training data.
definition: Srivastava and colleagues' 2014 regularization technique that randomly drops units and their connections during training to prevent co-adaptation and overfitting.
name: Dropout (2014)
source_title: Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting

causal_claim: Adam optimizer made the Transformer architecture possible by being the optimizer, with a warmup-and-decay learning-rate schedule, used to train the original Transformer, whose sparse and non-stationary gradients plain stochastic gradient descent handled poorly.
definition: Kingma and Ba's Adam, submitted in December 2014, a first-order stochastic optimizer computing per-parameter adaptive learning rates from estimates of the first and second moments of the gradients.
name: Adam optimizer (2014)
source_title: Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization

causal_claim: Perceptron made the Transformer architecture possible by originating the weighted-sum-plus-nonlinearity unit and the learnable-weight paradigm that, stacked and differentiated, become the Transformer's feed-forward layers.
definition: Frank Rosenblatt's perceptron, publicly demonstrated in July 1958, a single-layer neural network that learned to classify inputs by adjusting its connection weights.
name: Perceptron (1958)
source_title: Professor's perceptron paved the way for AI – 60 years too soon

causal_claim: Long short-term memory (LSTM) made the Transformer architecture possible by defining the state of the art it had to beat and exposing the exact bottleneck named in its motivation: even gated recurrence processes tokens sequentially, so the Transformer replaced recurrence with self-attention to gain parallel training on long contexts.
definition: Hochreiter and Schmidhuber's 1997 recurrent architecture using constant error carousels and multiplicative gates to learn dependencies over more than 1,000 time steps.
name: Long short-term memory (LSTM) (1997)

causal_claim: Neural probabilistic language model made the Transformer architecture possible by introducing learned word embeddings as the input representation of a neural sequence model, the embedding layer every Transformer still begins with.
definition: Bengio and colleagues' 2003 model that learns a distributed vector representation for each word jointly with a neural probability function over word sequences.
name: Neural probabilistic language model (2003)

causal_claim: Word2vec embeddings made the Transformer architecture possible by proving at scale that words as dense vectors support arithmetic semantic structure, validating the token-embedding representation on which the Transformer's attention operates.
definition: Mikolov and colleagues' 2013 continuous bag-of-words and skip-gram models for efficiently learning high-quality continuous word vectors from billions of words.
name: Word2vec embeddings (2013)
source_title: Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space

causal_claim: Sequence-to-sequence learning made the Transformer architecture possible by supplying the encoder-decoder template and the machine-translation task framing the Transformer kept, while its fixed-length vector bottleneck was the specific limitation that self-attention across all encoder positions was designed to remove.
definition: Sutskever, Vinyals and Le's 2014 end-to-end approach using one multilayer LSTM to encode an input sequence into a fixed-dimensional vector and another LSTM to decode the target sequence.
name: Sequence-to-sequence learning (2014)
source_title: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks
